intermediate.question: What is a UTXO?

options.text: An Unspent Transaction Output — a discrete 'chunk' of bitcoin you own that hasn't been spent yet
A type of Bitcoin wallet app
A unit used only for measuring mining power
A fee paid to the Bitcoin network

intermediate.question: When you spend bitcoin, what typically happens to the UTXO(s) used?

options.text: They are split in half automatically
They are consumed entirely and new UTXOs are created (including any 'change' sent back to you)
They remain unchanged and reusable
They are converted into a single account balance

intermediate.question: What is the mempool?

options.text: A waiting area where unconfirmed transactions sit before being included in a block
The total supply of bitcoin still to be mined
A backup copy of the blockchain
A wallet used by miners only

intermediate.question: Why might a transaction sit in the mempool for a long time without confirming?

options.text: The network is offline
The sender used a fee that's too low compared to current demand for block space
The recipient hasn't accepted it yet
Transactions always take the same fixed amount of time

intermediate.question: What drives Bitcoin's fee market?

options.text: A fixed government-set rate
Competition among users for limited block space — higher fees tend to get priority
The total number of bitcoin a wallet holds
The age of the wallet sending the transaction

intermediate.question: What is a multisig (multi-signature) wallet?

options.text: A wallet that requires multiple private keys to authorize a transaction, instead of just one
A wallet that can hold multiple cryptocurrencies at once
A wallet with multiple public addresses for receiving only
A wallet that automatically signs up for multiple exchanges

intermediate.question: A '2-of-3' multisig setup means:

options.text: Any 2 of the 3 designated keys must sign to approve a transaction
All 3 keys must always sign together
The wallet is limited to 3 transactions total
3 different people share one single key

intermediate.question: What is the Lightning Network?

options.text: A separate cryptocurrency that replaces Bitcoin
A 'layer 2' network built on top of Bitcoin that enables fast, low-fee payments
A faster version of Bitcoin mining hardware
A backup system for storing seed phrases

intermediate.question: Why was the Lightning Network created?

options.text: To replace Bitcoin's blockchain entirely
To enable faster and cheaper everyday payments without every transaction needing to go on the base blockchain
To increase Bitcoin's total supply
To eliminate the need for wallets

intermediate.question: In simple terms, what is a Lightning payment channel?

options.text: A two-party agreement that lets participants send many instant payments back and forth off-chain, settling on the blockchain only when needed
A physical cable connecting two mining rigs
A subscription that unlocks lower blockchain fees
A public chatroom for Bitcoin traders

intermediate.question: What's the key difference between a custodial and a non-custodial wallet, in terms of risk?

options.text: There is no risk difference between them
With a custodial wallet, you depend on a third party's solvency and security; with non-custodial, you bear full responsibility for your own keys
Custodial wallets are always illegal
Non-custodial wallets require a monthly fee to a company

intermediate.question: What is a hardware wallet?

options.text: A physical device designed to store private keys offline, isolated from internet-connected devices
A metal plate used to engrave your public address
A mining rig used to earn new bitcoin
A wallet app that only works on desktop computers

intermediate.question: What is a 'watch-only' wallet?

options.text: A wallet that can view balances and transactions using public keys/addresses, but cannot spend funds since it holds no private keys
A wallet used exclusively to monitor other people's transactions
A wallet that locks automatically after 60 seconds
A wallet that only works with Lightning payments

intermediate.question: What is the 'difficulty adjustment' in Bitcoin?

options.text: A periodic change to how hard it is to mine a new block, keeping average block time around 10 minutes as total mining power changes
A vote on whether to raise Bitcoin's price
A change to the maximum supply of bitcoin
A setting users adjust in their own wallet

intermediate.question: If more miners join the network and total computing power rises, what happens to mining difficulty?

options.text: It decreases
It stays exactly the same forever
It increases, to keep block production time roughly constant
Bitcoin's supply cap increases in response

intermediate.question: What does 'hash rate' refer to?

options.text: The total number of Bitcoin wallets in existence
The combined computational power being used to mine and secure the Bitcoin network
The percentage of bitcoin currently held on exchanges
The number of transactions per second

intermediate.question: What's the difference between a 'node' and a 'miner' in Bitcoin?

options.text: They are two names for the exact same role
A node validates and relays transactions/blocks according to the rules; a miner additionally competes to create new blocks. All miners run node software, but not all nodes mine
A node only exists on exchanges; miners only exist in wallets
A miner enforces rules, while a node only stores price data

intermediate.question: What does it mean to run a 'full node'?

options.text: Downloading and independently verifying the entire Bitcoin blockchain and its rules
Owning the maximum allowed amount of bitcoin
Operating a mining farm with many machines
Subscribing to a premium wallet service

intermediate.question: In general terms, what is a soft fork?

options.text: A backward-compatible upgrade to Bitcoin's rules, where old software can still recognize new blocks as valid
A permanent split that creates two separate cryptocurrencies
A change that doubles the block size
A reversal of a confirmed transaction

intermediate.question: In general terms, what is a hard fork?

options.text: A minor bug fix that requires no coordination
A rule change that is NOT backward-compatible, which can split the network into two separate chains if not everyone upgrades
A change only miners are allowed to vote on
A required annual software update

intermediate.question: Why do security experts recommend never entering your seed phrase into a website or app that requests it unexpectedly?

options.text: It's a common phishing tactic to steal full access to your wallet
Websites are legally required to store it for you
It's needed to verify your email address
It automatically converts your bitcoin to cash

intermediate.question: What is a common warning sign of a Bitcoin investment scam?

options.text: A platform clearly disclosing risks and fees
Guaranteed, risk-free returns or pressure to invest quickly
A wallet that lets you view your own transaction history
A hardware wallet requiring a PIN to unlock

intermediate.question: What is a 'dust' transaction generally understood to be?

options.text: A transaction sending an amount so small it may cost more in fees than it's worth
A transaction that fails validation
A transaction sent to a mining pool
A transaction between two exchanges

intermediate.question: What is a mining pool?

options.text: A group of miners who combine computing power and share the block rewards proportionally
A single company that owns all Bitcoin mining rights
A wallet designed only for miners
A fund that buys bitcoin on behalf of investors

intermediate.question: Why might someone choose a non-custodial wallet despite the added personal responsibility?

options.text: To avoid counterparty risk — no third party can freeze, lose, or misuse their funds
Because it's required by law in most countries
Because it eliminates the need for a seed phrase
Because it guarantees faster transaction confirmations

intermediate.question: What does 'block space' refer to?

options.text: The limited amount of data capacity available in each block for transactions
The physical storage size of a hardware wallet
The number of confirmed blocks in Bitcoin's history
The area on an exchange reserved for large trades

intermediate.question: What is 'fee bumping' (e.g., via Replace-By-Fee)?

options.text: Increasing the fee on an unconfirmed transaction to encourage faster confirmation
A penalty applied for sending too many transactions
A discount applied automatically after your first transaction
A fee charged only when withdrawing from an exchange

intermediate.question: What is 'address reuse' and why is it generally discouraged?

options.text: Using the same address repeatedly, which can make it easier for outside observers to link your transactions together
Sending bitcoin to an address that has already expired
A technical error that prevents a transaction from processing
A required step to verify wallet ownership

intermediate.question: In the context of Lightning, what is 'routing'?

options.text: Sending a payment across a path of connected channels between multiple parties, without needing a direct channel to the final recipient
Choosing which mining pool processes your transaction
Selecting which exchange handles your trade
Splitting a payment across multiple blockchains

intermediate.question: What is 'self-custody'?

options.text: Holding your own private keys and taking direct responsibility for securing your bitcoin, rather than relying on a third party
A legal service that manages your bitcoin for you
A feature exclusive to mining pools
A backup wallet provided free by exchanges
